#4550. Children made some of the Middle East’s oldest known clay figures

Published Nov 11, 2026 2:00 PM EST

About 10,000 years ago, a Neolithic culture in the southern Levant known as the Natufians became some of the first nomadic hunter-gatherers to transition towards agriculture. But even before this monumental lifestyle shift, members of the prehistoric community were already crafting symbolic figures from clay. What’s more, archaeologists say more than 150 recently discovered artifacts dating back 11,500 to 15,000 years ago are likely the earliest examples of their kind ever found in the Middle East. Their findings, published today in the journal PLOS One, suggest that even children sometimes had a role in creating these miniatures.

The Natufians lived in what is now known as the Fertile Crescent between 9,500 and 13,000 BCE. Pre-agrarian and semi-sedentary, the culture likely preceded the region’s first permanent Neolithic settlements. Although archaeologists previously located small figurines linked to the Natufians made from rocks and bones, these clay artifacts have larger implications. Crafting items from preexisting hard materials typically relies on intentionally shaping through processes like breaking, sanding, or whittling. The existence of clay items suggests that the Natufians didn’t just express themselves artistically and symbolically. They did so through materials that required additional steps like baking and hardening.

“This shift required diverse tools, skills, and knowledge, different from those needed for the manipulation of stone and bone,” the study’s authors wrote.

The figurines found at sites across present-day Israel include depictions of animals like birds and hooved mammals like deer, as well as both male and female individuals. Some of the pieces exhibit traces of pigment and other dyes, while others still feature ancient fingerprints of the artists themselves. Further examinations of these indentations shows that clay sculpting was an intergenerational craft, with both children and adults taking part in the activity.

“Thousands of years before agriculture and pottery emerged, people were already using clay to create figures, as part of their beliefs and knowledge of the natural world,” Laurent Davin, a study co-author and archaeologist at The Hebrew University of Jerusalem, said in a statement. “What is particularly fascinating is the evidence that children were involved in making these objects, suggesting that creativity and cultural knowledge were shared across generations.”

#4548. Tesla’s China sales crash 66% to lowest level in over four years

Only 8,817 of the cars Tesla delivered from Giga Shanghai in October went to Chinese buyers. That’s down 66% from a year ago and Tesla’s worst month in China since July 2022, according to CPCA data.

Back in July 2022, the Shanghai factory was partly shut down for line upgrades. This time it ran normally and shipped 87% of what it built out of the country.

The China Passenger Car Association (CPCA) reported that Tesla China wholesaled 67,829 vehicles in October, up 10.3% year-over-year. That’s the number most headlines ran with.

But 59,012 of those were exports. Strip them out and you’re left with 8,817 cars for the domestic market, the one Giga Shanghai was originally built to serve.

Nearly all of them were Model Ys (7,807), according to CnEVPost, leaving just 1,010 Model 3s. And compared to September, when Tesla sold 64,837 cars in China, domestic sales fell 86%.

Here’s how October has looked over the last three years:

Tesla favors export orders early in each quarter and pushes domestic deliveries toward the end of it, and September’s promotions and quarter-end rush pulled some demand forward.

That’s real. Tesla’s China sales have followed this sawtooth pattern for years. Last October was also weak, and Tesla then delivered 73,145 cars in China in November and 93,843 in December.

But it doesn’t explain the size of this drop. Here’s every first month of a quarter in 2026:

October is less than half of the previous low this year. And the October trough keeps getting deeper: 40,485 in 2024, 26,006 in 2025, 8,817 now.

China’s EV market is having a rough year. NEV retail sales fell 10% year-over-year in October to 1.148 million units, according to CPCA’s preliminary data, as Beijing phases out trade-in subsidies and the NEV purchase tax exemption was cut in half on January 1. The overall passenger car market was down 25%.

Tesla was down 66%. That works out to about 0.8% of China’s NEV retail market last month.

Meanwhile, Xiaomi, which only started delivering cars in 2024, delivered more than 50,000 vehicles in October. Leapmotor delivered 106,127, up 51%. BYD delivered 490,168, though that includes its exports.

Through October, Tesla has sold 389,905 cars in China. That’s down 15% from 458,710 over the same period last year and its lowest January-to-October total in at least four years:

The decline is speeding up. Tesla was down 11.9% in China through September, and one bad October pushed that to 15%. This year is now 22% below the 2024 peak, or about 110,000 fewer cars.

Exports from Giga Shanghai went the other way, up 101% to 420,984.

So this year, Shanghai has now shipped more cars abroad than it sold at home. Last year, domestic sales beat exports by more than two to one.

As we reported last month, Beijing is cutting the VAT export rebate on EVs from 13% to 9% on April 1, 2027, with the rate set by the customs declaration date. We said to expect automakers to cram exports in ahead of the deadline. October’s 59,012 exports, up 66% year-over-year, fit that.

We’ve been tracking this gap all year, from Tesla’s Q1 China retail crash to the first-half numbers. Every time, the wholesale headline looks fine and the domestic number underneath gets worse. October is the most extreme version yet: Tesla China “grew” 10% while Chinese buyers bought 66% fewer Teslas.

We don’t buy that this is just the quarterly cycle. The cycle explains why October is weaker than September. It doesn’t explain why this October is a third of last October, or less than half of any other month this year.

I've been saying this for the last two years. Tesla's problem isn't that Elon temporarily alienated customers in Europe or other countries. Yes that killed sales for a bit, but in the end people are practical and will buy the best car for the money. And we saw that is exactly what happened with European Tesla sales coming back when gas prices rose and Tesla as a package (quality + price) was still very competitive.

The real problem that Tesla has is that they're falling behind in China not because anyone cares about Elon's politics, but because the cars are just less and less competitive. And while the Chinese competition doubles down on vehicle development and rolls out a new car every week, Tesla has lost all interest in it. There is absolutely nothing on the horizon for them in terms of new vehicles that consumers can buy. Looks like the 3 and Y are all they will have and no updates are coming.

I know, FSD or bust, but that's also assuming Chinese brands don't crack that nut at the same time.

Two things can be true at once. The export numbers show Tesla front-loading shipments ahead of the rebate cut. And Chinese demand for a Model 3 and Model Y lineup that hasn’t fundamentally changed in years keeps fading while Xiaomi, Leapmotor and BYD launch new models every few months.

And if Tesla is choosing to send cars abroad instead of selling them in China, that’s not exactly a vote of confidence in its Chinese business either.

The real test is November and December. Last year, Tesla bounced back to 73,000 and 94,000 domestic sales. If it gets close to that again, October was mostly timing. If it doesn’t, Tesla has a serious problem in the world’s largest EV market, and the export valve that’s been hiding it gets more expensive in April.

#4547. Honda Investing $3 Billion to Build New Ohio Factory, Increase Hybrid Production in U.S.

The new plant will be capable of producing 240,000 vehicles a year, and multiple new models are currently under development.

Audi may have recently announced its first-ever U.S. production facility, but at least one Japanese automaker with a head start in that race doesn’t seem keen on giving up any places. On Monday, Honda announced it is investing $3 billion in a new central Ohio factory; the plant, which will produce up to 240,000 vehicles annually, is expected to be online by 2029.

Now, with nine production facilities across the U.S., Honda is no stranger to domestic production, but the new factory plan goes beyond merely adding production capacity. Instead, the company is targeting increased production of hybrid-electric vehicles and their accompanying drivetrain parts. The new plant will sit between Honda’s current East Liberty and Marysville Auto Plants, the carmaker said, and will focus on multiple vehicle types and powertrains, including hybrid and battery-electric vehicles. Honda said the plant will be one of the most advanced factories in the world, leveraging leading-edge automation, data-driven technologies and flexible production systems.

"As Honda approaches 50 years of building products close to our customers in America, we are making one of the most significant commitments in our history to position Honda for the next 50 years,” said Bob Nelson, executive vice president of American Honda Motor Co., Inc. “These investments strengthen America’s role as a cornerstone of Honda’s global future and reflect our confidence in our more than 30,000 Honda associates and the strength of American manufacturing. By expanding our comprehensive R&D and manufacturing capabilities, we will be better positioned to serve our customers and contribute to the economic vitality of the communities where we operate.”

Building another plant in Ohio was an easy choice for Honda. Honda’s U.S. supply base is nearby, and the automaker has a strong reputation among the region’s skilled workforce. The Japanese automaker has previously committed to launching 15 new Honda and Acura hybrid models globally by 2030; North America is the target for many of these models, which are currently in development at R&D facilities in California and Ohio. All told, Honda said the new plant will increase its annual U.S. production capacity to approximately 1.3 million vehicles a year.

The company’s Alabama Auto Plant will also receive new investment to expand engine production for a new V-6 hybrid engine; Honda will retool the engine production facility and one of the production lines to accommodate Passport SUV production. The Anna Engine Plant in Ohio will also be retooled, to produce a next-generation 4-cylinder Atkinson-cycle engine for future compact and midsize vehicles built in North America. Honda Transmission Plant-Ohio will be retooled for two next-generation Honda Hybrid systems in compact vehicles, while Honda Transmission Plant-Georgia will be retooled for next-generation hybrid systems in larger vehicles. All this retooling will account for a 250-percent increase in hybrid powertrain system capacity in Ohio.

“Honda's leadership could have chosen to build this plant anywhere in the world, but they chose Ohio because there are so many advantages to being here,” said Ohio governor Mike DeWine. “For almost half a century, Honda and Ohio have grown together, and generations of families have built their careers on Honda's manufacturing lines. Today's announcement isn't just an investment in a new facility—it's an investment in Ohio's people and Ohio's future.”

#4546. Every EV from Every Brand in America

We've created this handy guide to let you know all the brands that sell electric vehicles in the United States.

While gas-powered vehicles still make up an overwhelming majority of cars sold in the United States, their market share is slowly getting chipped away at by battery-electric ones. Since the Nissan Leaf and Tesla Roadster brought electric vehicles back to the national stage in the late 2000s, automakers have worked overtime to noticeably improve the charging speeds and driving ranges of their battery-powered products. No longer limited to small cars, EVs now take up space in just about every automotive segment.

We've compiled an exhaustive list of today's options to make it easy to determine what electric vehicles are available from which automotive brands in the United States. Don't go looking for hydrogen-powered electric vehicles here, though, as we've excluded those from this list.

Audi sells an array of electric SUVs and cars, from the compact Q4 e-tron to the range-topping 912-hp RS e-tron GT. Both of Audi's electric SUVs are available in either wagon or fastback body styles.

BMW's EV sedans look similar to their gas-powered cars, but the iX3 and incoming i3 promise next-generation looks and technology.

Cadillac's lineup of electric vehicles consists of an SUV in nearly every size, including the Escalade IQ, which looks just as ostentatious as the gas-powered Escalade despite its silent powertrain.

Chevrolet's electric vehicle arsenal is centered around SUVs, but the American automaker also caters to business owners with the WT version of the Silverado EV pickup truck.

Dodge currently sells just one EV, the Charger Daytona, which is available as either a coupe or sedan. It assumes the muscle car role vacated by the previous Scat Pack and Hellcat versions of the Charger and Challenger.

The only Fiat sold in the United States right now is an electric version of the company's iconic 500 city car. Fiat also offers the Topolino, which is technically classified as a "Low Speed Vehicle" and is limited to 25 mph.

Ford sells two electric models, the Mustang Mach-E SUV and the E-Transit commercial van.

The Genesis Electrified GV70 is based on the Korean automaker's popular compact SUV, while the GV60 utilizes the same platform found under the Hyundai Ioniq 5 and Kia EV6.

GMC's lineup of electric vehicles is just as big and brash as its gas-powered offerings. Two pickups and an SUV are available.

Hyundai has won Car and Driver's EV of the Year award three times in a row, first with the Ioniq 5 SUV in 2022 and then with the Ioniq 6 sedan in 2023. The high-powered Ioniq 5 N, which entertains with faux gearshifts and engine noises, won the award in 2024.

Jeep currently sells two EVs in the U.S. Although the Wagoneer S shares the first part of its name with the gas-powered Wagoneer, the EV is completely unrelated to that behemoth. The Recon is an electric alternative to the off-road-ready Wrangler.

Kia's lineup of EVs currently consists of a trio of SUVs.

Lexus currently sells two EVs in the United States: the RZ SUV, which is related to the Toyota bZ, and an electric version of the ES sedan.

California-based startup Lucid Motors exclusively builds EVs and recently launched its second model, the Gravity SUV.

The Italian luxury brand currently offers three EVs in the U.S., all of which are related to the brand's gas-powered models and carry the Folgore suffix to distinguish them as battery-powered.

Mercedes offers a vast range of EVs, from sedans to SUVs and even vans. The automaker has begun shifting away from its "EQ" naming structure for EVs, starting with the electric G-class, which dons the name G580 with EQ Technology. It's a wordy solution that'll also appear on the upcoming battery-electric 2026 CLA-class.

While Mini previously sold an electric variation of its iconic Cooper hatchback, the latest version has been delayed indefinitely, meaning Mini currently offers just one EV in the U.S., a battery-powered variant of its Countryman SUV

Nissan sells one EV in the United States, the Leaf, which has transformed from a hatchback to an SUV for its third generation.

There are currently three Porsche EVs on sale in the U.S., with an electric successor to its 718 sports car on the way.

Ram, the truck division spun off from Dodge in 2009, currently sells one EV. Ram had originally aimed to start building the 1500 REV in late 2024 for deliveries in early 2025, but the electric pickup truck is now delayed to late 2026.

#4545. The coolest ride in town is England’s first electric ice cream truck

The “world’s leading ice cream truck manufacturer” has released its first fully electric ice cream truck, which is already in operaiton, and it says it’s open for orders for more.

Whitby Morrison bills itself as “the world’s leading ice cream truck manufacturer,” supplying converted vans as ice cream trucks to drivers worldwide.

And now it has taken a big step into the modern age delivering its first fully electric ice cream truck to Hocking’s dairy in North Devon, England.

The truck has been operating since July, through the course of one “ice cream season.” It reportedly covered more than 100 miles a day and has done days serving up to 12 hours at a time.

It’s built on a standard Mercedes eSprinter, so it’s not retrofitted from the diesel vans that make up most of Whitby Morrison’s other offerings. The eSprinter comes in a “chassis cab” configuration which comes with just the chassis and cab, and lets upfitters build whatever they want onto the back end of the vehicle.

In this case, it also got some pretty extensive (and a little over-the-top) art all around the vehicle, highlighting the van’s electric operation.

The ice cream truck maker, Whitby Morrison, says this is the “world’s first fully certified electric ice cream truck.”

We’re not sure what sort of international certifications are required for an ice cream truck so we’ll take their word for it, but we have seen a Rivian EDV turned into a Ben & Jerry’s ice cream truck, complete with side window, and a concept electric ice cream truck as far back as 2019. So it’s certainly not the very first time this idea has been had, at least.

And it is a good idea. As with school buses, ice cream trucks are vehicles that children are likely to congregate around. Having a stinky old truck spewing emissions just a few feet away from those kids’ lungs is the sort of thing that can expose them to a life of health problems… and we might as well not stack that on top of the sugar addiction we’re teaching them to have (hey, at least they have to get outside to chase the truck down, so they’re getting some physical activity out of it, right?)

It also opens up more possibilities for operators to serve at events where having a diesel truck running might not be reasonable, like in enclosed spaces or where quiet might be appreciated (this came up when we went to Harbinger Motors’ factory opening, where local food trucks were in attendance, inside the large factory building, and made the air quality noticeably worse).

Whitby Morrison says it’s taking orders both in the UK and overseas, with US orders just opening. To learn more, head on over to its website.

If you’ve been saving money for Black Friday, there has been a change of plans. Every year, Barnes & Noble slashes prices on Criterion collection movies and box sets by half. It’s the next best thing to being in the Criterion Closet. Most of the bestselling single-film 4K discs in the Criterion sale are $24.99, the bestselling standard Blu-rays are mostly $19.99, and the big director box sets are half off too. B&N ships orders of $60 or more for free, so three of the $24.99 4K discs clear the bar. The discount doesn’t stack with B&N’s Premium Membership discount, and a few of the most popular new 4K releases are already out of stock online. We checked every price and stock status in this post on Barnes & Noble Wednesday afternoon, November 11.

A family movie night pick that holds up for the grown-ups

Plenty of family movies wear thin for the adults in the room by the fifth viewing, but The Princess Bride keeps getting quoted at dinner tables for a reason. The Criterion edition of The Princess Bride is $24.99 at Barnes & Noble, half of its $49.99 list price. B&N lists it as a 4K Ultra HD and Blu-ray combo, so the standard disc covers any player in the house that can’t handle 4K. Rob Reiner’s 1987 fairy tale is a good place to start if you’re building a disc collection for a family that mostly streams.

The Coens’ Best Picture winner on 4K disc

Javier Bardem’s coin-flipping hitman is one of the scariest villains of the century, and the film around him won Best Picture. The No Country for Old Men 4K Blu-ray is $24.99, down from $49.99. Joel and Ethan Coen’s 2007 West Texas chase also stars Josh Brolin as the hunter who stumbles onto $2 million in drug money and Tommy Lee Jones as the sheriff trying to keep up.

Akira Kurosawa made Yojimbo in 1961 and followed it with Sanjuro a year later, both starring Toshiro Mifune as the same scruffy, sharp-witted ronin. The Yojimbo/Sanjuro 4K Blu-ray set puts both films on 4K for $39.99, which works out to about $20 per movie. If Yojimbo’s plot sounds familiar, that’s because Sergio Leone borrowed it for A Fistful of Dollars. This set pairs well with the Seven Samurai 4K Blu-ray, which is $29.99.

Ten films, 20 discs and more than 25 hours of extras

This is the splurge pick in the sale, but per film it costs about the same as the single 4K discs and adds a Blu-ray copy of each movie. The Wes Anderson Archive: Ten Films, Twenty-Five Years is $249.99, half of its $499.99 list price, which comes to $25 per film. Criterion says the set includes ten 4K UHD discs in Dolby Vision HDR, ten Blu-rays and more than 25 hours of special features, running from Bottle Rocket through The French Dispatch. Every film in the set has new 4K masters supervised and approved by Anderson, according to Criterion.

The Princess Bride, No Country for Old Men and Yojimbo/Sanjuro are covered above. Most of the bestselling single-film 4K discs are $24.99, including Wall-E and David Lynch’s Mulholland Dr. A few older classics, like Citizen Kane, are $29.99. You need a 4K player to watch these discs, and our guide to the best Blu-ray players covers the 4K models worth buying.

The bestselling standard Blu-rays are mostly $19.99, and they play on any Blu-ray player or game console with a disc drive. The KPop Demon Hunters Blu-ray is $19.99 and the KPop Demon Hunters DVD is $14.99, though its 4K edition is out of stock online. Bong Joon-ho’s Parasite is also $19.99.

The Wes Anderson Archive and Yojimbo/Sanjuro are covered above. Box sets get the same 50 percent cut as single discs, and the big director collections are where the dollar savings add up. The 30-disc Ingmar Bergman’s Cinema set is $149.99, and the Essential Fellini set is $124.99.

#4543. Stolen McLaren 750S Spotted Doing Donuts at Detroit Street Takeover, Tracked Down Via Social Media

The McLaren's owner put his 1.1 million followers to work tracking down his purloined supercar.

If you’re going to steal a bright green McLaren 750S, you might want to try to keep a low profile. At least, as low a profile as can be possible in a supercar. Doing donuts at a street takeover in front of a crowd of spectators, then, is probably not the best idea.

According to ClickOnDetroit, this indeed happened. The McLaren in question belonged to Ali Sobh, a Detroit businessman and social media influencer with approximately 1.1 million followers. The exotic car was reportedly stolen from a driveway behind his home in Detroit's historic Boston-Edison neighborhood. Sobh was understandably upset when he realized his prized possession was taken; however, salt arrived in the wound when he saw a video circulating online showing his McLaren spinning donuts in front of spectators, many of whom were recording the spectacle on their phones.

So, Sobh turned to his social media followers for help locating the McLaren. Tips began coming in, eventually providing a possible location near Six Mile Road and Telegraph Road. Sobh passed that information along to Detroit police, who subsequently recovered the car.

Getting the McLaren back is obviously a big win, but that’s not the end of the story. Detroit police are reviewing footage from the street takeover and working to identify those responsible for the theft. Authorities have not announced any arrests, and it's unclear whether the person performing donuts was involved in stealing the vehicle.

Sobh claims his car is worth approximately $500,000, and he doesn’t ever want it stolen again, so he says plans to improve security around his home to prevent that from happening. In the meantime, it must be reassuring to know that he can count on more than one million followers to help him out when things go south.

#4541. 2027 VinFast VF8

See all results for new 2027 VinFast VF8 for sale near 89109

VinFast is probably a brand name you’ve not heard before, and that’s because the Vietnam-based company has been selling electric SUVs here for only a few years. The VF8, introduced in 2023, hasn’t sold in significant numbers. In fact, there were no 2026 VF8s, but after skipping a model year, it's back for 2027.

The VF8 is compelling on paper, with a long list of standard amenities and an attractive starting price. All models are all-wheel drive and feature two electric motors generating 349 or 402 horsepower, depending on trim. It's on the road where things quickly fall apart. The VF8’s road manners are rough, its driving range is uncompetitive with similarly priced rival EV SUVs, and its onboard infotainment tech is a nightmare of unintuitive menus and software bugs.

Expert Tip: If an affordable, scienced-out electric SUV with decent range and a long warranty is what you’re after, consider the Hyundai Ioniq 5 or the Kia EV6 instead.

After taking the 2026 model year off, the VF8 is back, sporting a lower starting price. The Eco trim’s $41,790 ask represents a $5410 drop from the 2025 model, and the Plus’s $46,990 price is $6010 less than it was previously. VinFast has improved the VF8’s driver-assistance offerings this year too, adding rear automated emergency braking, an intersection assist system, an automatic lane-changing feature, evasive steering assist, and a feature that will bring the car to a stop if it detects that the driver has become unresponsive.

If this year's model is largely unchanged and you're comfortable with a lightly used car, you may want to consider shopping previous model years. A one-to-three-year-old model will likely have a warranty and it'll cost less than buying new.

An all-wheel-drive electric powertrain with two electric motors makes 349 horsepower in the Eco trim and 402 horsepower in the Plus model. While acceleration is respectable for a compact electric SUV, the VF8 falls short in other, subjective areas. For example, the VF8 we sampled was bouncy on uneven roads and its steering required too much effort.

In Comparison: The VF8 Plus’s 60 mph time in our testing is a half second behind the less powerful, 320-hp Hyundai Ioniq 5.

In Comparison: The VF8’s 3,968-pound towing capacity is stout, and although hooking up a trailer of that weight will reduce overall driving range, it is a higher maximum capacity than rivals such as the Ford Mustang Mach-E and the Hyundai Ioniq 5.

As its name suggests, the Eco model can go further on a single charge with an estimated range of 256 miles. The Plus model is rated at 224 miles of range. The VF8’s range figures lag other competitors in the segment. Similarly priced versions of the Tesla Model Y offer ranges stretching as high as 355 miles per charge. When plugged into a DC fast-charger, VinFast claims that the VF8’s battery can charge from 10 to 70 percent in just 31 minutes.

The EPA estimates that the VF8 Eco is good for 77 MPGe city, 69 MPGe highway, and 73 MPGe combined; the Plus model is rated for 75 MPGe city, 71 MPGe highway, and 73 MPGe combined. When we have a chance to take a VF8 on our 75-mph highway fuel economy route, we'll update this story with real-world test results. For more information about the VF8's fuel economy, visit the EPA's website.

First Row: The VF8's interior presentation is simple and minimalistic, tossing out traditional driver-facing gauges in favor of a head-up display. Unfortunately, the interior looks more premium than it feels to the touch, and we found the model we drove to be noisy over rough pavement. There are plenty of amenities, though, even in the base Eco trim. Heated front seats, a heated steering wheel, dual-zone automatic climate control, and faux leather upholstery are standard on all trims.

Second Row: Both rows of seats take full advantage of the space available, and the VF8 feels roomy inside. A pair of adults of above-average height will find plenty of legroom and headroom in the back seat. The Plus trim comes with heated outboard rear seats.

Cargo Capacity: The VF8 does offer a commendable amount of storage, though, with both a traditional rear hatch area and a frunk. In our testing, we fit eight carry-on suitcases in the VF8’s cargo bay; with the rear seats folded, we fit a total of 24.

A large 15.6-inch dashboard-mounted display shows vehicle information and doubles as a digital gauge display. For drivers who prefer to have critical information in front of them, a configurable head-up display comes standard and can project information such as speed, state of charge, and navigation onto the windshield. After getting a chance to use the VF8’s infotainment system, we noted that it was laggy and unintuitive compared to that of other vehicles, which will frustrate anyone expecting response speeds and user-friendly navigation of a smartphone.

All VF8 models come with a comprehensive package of driver-assistance features, including conveniences such as automatic high-beam headlamps and traffic sign recognition. In our experience, they worked well, but if you want to turn them off, you'll have to do it each time on startup, which is annoying. Even then, the VF8 will beep and boop with alerts as you approach lane markings or accidentally get too close to another car in traffic.

For information about the VF8’s crash-test results, visit the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) and Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) websites.

VinFast offers a generous 10-year/125,000-mile warranty, which should help assuage the fears that come with taking on the risk of buying an electric SUV from an unknown brand. Only Genesis, Kia, and Hyundai come close to VinFast's powertrain warranty with their 10-year policy that extends to 100,000 miles.

#4540. Juiced unveils another lower-cost moto-styled electric bike: Scrambler Core

Juiced Bikes is expanding its recently relaunched Scrambler lineup with a new, more affordable model known as the Juiced Scrambler Core. The new bike keeps much of the moto-inspired styling and performance of the existing Scrambler Hardtail, but trims back several components to knock several hundred dollars off the price.

The new Scrambler Core starts at $1,399, compared to $1,699 for the existing Scrambler Hardtail.

Juiced is also offering a $1,599 long-range version of the Core, as well as a smaller “Midsize” frame that should make the bike much more accessible to shorter riders – and, perhaps more importantly, teenagers.

Teens are a major part of the moto-style e-bike market, and Juiced has designed its Scrambler e-bikes as a safer option for those younger riders. In addition to ensuring street-legal performance for most major markets, Juiced rolled out a feature known as Speed Lock, which is essentially a parental control option that lets a parent or guardian set a lower speed limit using a PIN code that prevents their teen from later modifying the speed limit.

The launch comes as part of the rebirth of Juiced Bikes following the brand’s acquisition last year. The company was founded in 2009 and was acquired in 2025 by the co-founders of Lectric Ebikes, who have since brought the brand back with a new generation of its popular Scrambler platform.

The biggest changes appear to be in the powertrain, battery, brakes, and suspension.

The standard Scrambler Hardtail launched earlier this year set the standard for the flagship models by using a 750W nominal motor with 90 Nm of torque and reaching 28 mph (45 km/h). Its 52V 19.2Ah battery provides nearly 1 kWh of capacity and a claimed range of up to 60 miles (96 km).

The Scrambler Core steps down to a 500W nominal rear hub motor rated for 1,176W peak and 80 Nm of torque. Top speed is also reduced slightly to 25 mph (40 km/h), while the throttle is limited to 20 mph (32 km/h). Importantly, though, Juiced has retained its 52V architecture, meaning this is still a fairly punchy setup rather than a dramatically detuned budget bike.

Battery capacity takes a hit as well. The standard Core gets a 52V 10Ah battery with 520 Wh of capacity, rated for up to 40 miles (64 km) of range. Spending another $200 gets the Core Long-Range with a 52V 15Ah, 780Wh battery and a claimed 60-mile (96 km) maximum range. As with nearly all e-bikes, expect real-world range to fall short of the idealized advertised numbers, which are generally only achievable under the lowest power pedal assist.

Juiced also traded the Talon P4 four-piston hydraulic brakes found on the more expensive Scrambler for Talon P2 two-piston brakes. The KKE inverted fork with 140mm of travel is gone too, replaced by a more conventional aluminum triple-crown fork with 100mm of travel.

Those are meaningful downgrades, but they’re also largely the kinds of changes I’d expect to see when trying to shave $300 off an already competitively priced moto-style e-bike. It’s a strategy we’ve seen play out before in the industry, helping lower costs for riders who want a flagship bike but don’t necessarily want to pay flagship prices.

Even so, important features remain to help maintain the look and feel of the Juiced Scrambler line. The Core still gets 20 x 4-inch fat tires, hydraulic disc brakes, a frame-integrated TFT display, four pedal-assist levels, a headlight, taillight, brake light, and turn signals. It’s a single-speed setup and weighs 73 lb (33 kg), while being rated for a 300 lb (136 kg) payload.

Perhaps the more interesting addition is the Scrambler Core Midsize.

While the regular Core is recommended for riders 5’2” and taller, the Midsize drops that figure to just 4’10”. Pricing remains the same: $1,399 with the 520Wh battery or $1,599 with the 780Wh long-range pack.

And with an eye towards safety, the Core and Core Mini retain Juiced’s PIN-protected parental speed lock. Parents can set the motor-assisted top speed anywhere from 1-25 mph and lock the setting behind a four-digit PIN. That makes even more sense on the Midsize version, which seems tailor-made for younger riders who want the moto-style look but may not yet comfortably fit the larger Scrambler.

The Core is launching in several decidedly Juiced color names, including Black Nectar, Fruit Punch, Sour Grape, White Grape, Berry Freeze, and Blood Orange, though availability varies between frame sizes and battery configurations. Juiced says preorders are expected to begin shipping around the end of the month.

At $1,399, the Scrambler Core feels like a logical extension of Juiced’s rebooted lineup. You lose some battery, motor power, braking hardware, suspension travel, and a few mph compared to the Hardtail, but the underlying recipe is largely intact. For riders who mostly want the Scrambler look and feel – or parents shopping for a smaller rider – saving $300 may be a pretty compelling trade. Especially when you consider that the original Juiced Scrambler already led the industry in value for moto-style e-bikes from reputable brands.

Toss in the strong backing from Lectric and the 3-year warranty, and it’s hard to consider much else among the competition.

#4539. A wobbly exoplanet vanished—but astronomers aren’t worried

Published Nov 11, 2026 4:01 PM EST

For the first time, astronomers witnessed a gigantic exoplanet dramatically vanish from view. But the “hot Jupiter” located about 1,000 light-years from Earth didn’t evaporate into the vacuum of space. Instead, the gravitational pull from an uncomfortably close neighbor is causing TOI-2535 b to wobble in its orbit thanks to the same dynamics dictating solar and lunar eclipses. The unusual discovery is detailed in a study recently published in Astrophysical Journal Letters, and relies on observations gathered by NASA’s Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) orbital telescope.

“We think of the universe as resembling clockwork, where everything is regular, but that’s not true,” Samuel Yee, a University of California Los Angeles (UCLA) astronomer and study co-author, explained in a recent profile. “If there are multiple planets in a system, they can affect each other’s orbits.”

Astronomers first began examining TOI-2535 b in April 2019 using TESS. The eagle-eyed telescope identifies new planets by flagging subtle changes in stellar brightness. These changes are often caused by a previously unknown planet’s transit in front of its star as seen from Earth. In some ways, TOI-2535 b resembles our solar system’s largest planet, but it is even closer to its own star than Mercury is to our sun. While Mercury takes 88 days to complete the trip, TOI-2535 b circles back around once every 8.25 days.

While using TESS to get glimpses of TOI-2535 b over the next seven years, researchers realized the hot Jupiter’s transits didn’t occur on a regular schedule like most other planets. Instead, the exoplanet’s light fluctuations could arrive upwards of six hours earlier or later than predicted. Over time, astronomers also noticed these transits become shallower and shorter. Then, in March, TOI-2535 b simply didn’t show up during the space telescope’s scan of the system.

Researchers including Yee now believe their hot Jupiter isn’t alone—it actually has an incredibly close gas giant neighbor with a comparatively tilted orbit. The two planets’ relationship causes them to essentially wobble like a pair of tops, eventually throwing one another out of alignment so that they disappear from Earth’s viewpoint.

“This is the most extreme example we’ve seen because the two planets are interacting so strongly,” said Yee. “The planet’s orbit is tilting so quickly that its transit disappeared while we were watching.”

The forces at play are the same as those that ensure eclipses don’t follow a regularly repeating cycle. UCLA astrophysicist and study co-author Erik Petigura explained that this is due to the moon’s tilted orbit, which comes from its cataclysmic early formation following a collision with Earth.

“If the moon’s orbit around the Earth was perfectly aligned with the Earth’s orbit around the sun, we would see an eclipse every month,” Petigura explained.

Yee, Petigura, and their colleagues are lucky to have spotted TOI-2535’s disappearing act when they did. Based on their calculations, its next transit in front of its star won’t occur for another 30 to 50 years—although they may see its partner planet sooner once it emerges from behind its stellar anchor.

#4538. John F. Kennedy Jr.’s Last Car, a 1994 Saab 900 Coupe, Is Going Up for Auction

And, yes, in case you were wondering, it is a five-speed manual.

If you’ve ever wanted to own an automotive piece of Kennedy family history, now’s your chance. John F. Kennedy Jr.’s last car, a 1994 Saab 900 SE Coupe, will be auctioned off Wednesday, November 11th at 7 p.m. EST by RR Auctions.

The dark green three-door coupe was the last vehicle Kennedy owned before he, his wife Carolyn Bessette Kennedy, and sister-in-law Lauren Bessette were killed in a plane crash off the coast of Martha’s Vineyard on July 16, 1999. As he purchased it new, Kennedy was able to have the Saab fitted with a light beige leather interior, a five-speed manual transmission, and a turquoise-green “Main Beach” roof rack. There’s only 30,650 miles on the odometer, and RR Auctions says the vehicle shows evidence of age and use, including wear on the leather upholstery and areas of soiling on the carpeting. A printed photograph of John F. Kennedy Jr. and Carolyn Bessette-Kennedy beside the Saab will be included.

“For a man born into one of America’s wealthiest and most famous families, Kennedy’s choice of a Saab was notably modest. He purchased the new 900 SE from Zumbach Sports Cars in Manhattan in the summer of 1994 for $29,841.21, equipped with such everyday conveniences as a CD player and phone hookup,” the listing reads. “The practical Swedish hatchback suited the understated, slightly unconventional style Kennedy cultivated as an adult, far removed from the ostentation his wealth and celebrity could have afforded him. He drove it regularly around New York, and the intensely photographed nature of his life made the Saab a recurring backdrop to his final years: numerous period images show Kennedy, and later Carolyn Bessette-Kennedy, with the car, sometimes attempting to make their way through the paparazzi who followed them through the city.”

The Saab sat at the Larchmont, New York home of Kennedy’s friend, Kevin Hynes, for days after the plane crash. Hynes bought the Saab from the Kennedy estate in 2000 for $6000; in 2006, Hynes sold the 900 Coupe to Michael Esposito for $12,000.

When the vehicle was photographed on July 23, 1999, its contents included a football, a soccer ball, a rope, automotive fluid, a March 1999 issue of Rolling Stone, and a Piper baseball cap. Some of these items have been auctioned off previously, but this is the first time the vehicle itself has appeared. An E-ZPass transponder, a handwritten telephone-message sheet, an Airborne Express receipt associated with the 2000 estate transaction, and a DeWitt Stern Group envelope addressed to “Mr. John F. Kennedy” and marked “PERSONAL & CONFIDENTIAL” will be included with the purchase.

As of publication, 24 bids have been placed on the 1994 Saab 900. The current bidding price is $26,575.

A New York transplant hailing from the Pacific Northwest, Emmet White has a passion for anything that goes: cars, bicycles, planes, and motorcycles. After learning to ride at 17, Emmet worked in the motorcycle industry before joining Autoweek in 2022 and Road & Track in 2024. The woes of alternate side parking have kept his fleet moderate, with a 2014 Volkswagen Jetta GLI and a BMW 318i E30 street parked in his Queens community.

#4537. 2027 Rivian Commercial Van

See all results for new 2027 Rivian Commercial Van for sale near 70005

Although it started off as an exclusive delivery van for Amazon, Rivian is now offering its electric Commercial Van (RCV) for sale to other fleet-based businesses. They don’t come painted in that gray-blue hue like the ones Prime members are accustomed to seeing as their packages get dropped off, but you can buy the same short-wheelbase Delivery 500 and long-wheelbase Delivery 700 variants as Amazon uses.

Rivian claims a driving range of up to 161 miles per charge for the Delivery 500 and 153 miles for the Delivery 700. Both models come with a single electric motor making 320 horsepower and driving the front wheels. The cabin is spartan but thoughtfully laid out, and the cargo area is vast and can be set up to accommodate a variety of business needs. We also think it could make a pretty slick vanlife conversion.

Expert Tip: Electric full-size vans are no longer a novelty, as Ford offers one called E-Transit and Mercedes-Benz makes an EV version of its Sprinter van called eSprinter.

Rivian has made no changes to the Commercial Van for the 2027 model year.

If this year's model is largely unchanged and you're comfortable with a lightly used car, you may want to consider shopping previous model years. A one-to-three-year-old model will likely have a warranty and it'll cost less than buying new.

Both versions of the Commercial Van are powered by a 320-hp electric motor that drives the front wheels. All-wheel drive is not an option. We haven't driven either van yet, but given how quickly Amazon drivers move about, we suspect the electric motor provides adequate acceleration, even when the back is fully loaded with cargo.

Though not intended for towing, the Delivery 500 can haul a decent bit of gear, with a payload of 2663 pounds and a cargo capacity of 487 cubic feet. The longer-wheelbase Delivery 700 offers 652 cubic feet of space but a significantly lower payload rating of 2258 pounds.

Rivian claims the Delivery 500 can go 161 miles on a charge, while the longer Delivery 700 has a maximum range of 153 miles. Both models use a lithium-iron-phosphate battery pack, capable of 100-kW fast- charging, and the vans have both J1772 and CCS ports.

The EPA doesn't publish fuel-economy numbers for commercial vehicles, and Rivian hasn't released estimates. If we get a chance, we'll take the RCV on our 75-mph highway fuel-economy route and update this story with real-world test results.

First Row: Like the exterior, the RCV's interior is simple yet modern. Behind the sliding front door is an elevated driver's chair and a chunky plastic dash that supports a flat-bottom steering wheel and two large screens—one for instruments and the other for infotainment. There's also a fold-down jump seat for the occasional passenger. The RV-like wraparound windshield provides good forward visibility, and a standard 360-degree camera system ensures the driver can see what's behind them.

Cargo Capacity: Behind the roll-up rear door is an empty cavity that fleet owners can spec with shelves and various flooring options. #4535. Garmin and Waze just teamed up on a clever new way to keep cyclists safer

Garmin and Waze are teaming up on an interesting new safety feature that could give cyclists a little extra protection when sharing the road with cars – by making cyclists themselves show up in Waze.

The new feature allows cyclists using a compatible Garmin Edge bike computer or Garmin smartwatch to share their location through Garmin’s LiveTrack feature. That location can then appear in real time to nearby drivers using Waze, with cyclists displayed as moving icons on the road.

As someone who recently joined the Garmin family myself with a smartwatch for tracking my cycling, running, and other activities, this is exactly the type of feature I love seeing added to the platform.

I’ve long maintained that safety – or more accurately, the perception that cycling isn’t safe – is one of the biggest impediments to getting more people onto bikes.

That’s especially true in the US, where cyclists are often forced to share roads with cars instead of enjoying the kind of widespread separated cycling infrastructure found in many more bike-friendly countries. And when a cyclist and a multi-ton vehicle have to occupy the same space, making sure the driver knows that cyclist is there can make a big difference.

Of course, an icon on Waze isn’t going to magically make cycling safe. It won’t replace protected bike lanes, better road design, slower vehicle speeds, or attentive drivers.

But I can certainly imagine situations where it could help. Riding at night or in poor visibility, approaching a blind curve, or simply traveling on a narrow road where a driver might otherwise come upon a cyclist unexpectedly are all situations where an advance warning could be useful.

The feature is opt-in through Garmin Connect and activates when the cyclist starts an outdoor cycling activity. Garmin says location sharing is temporary and session-based, and that cyclists’ personal information isn’t displayed in Waze. Of course, anyone who uses a personal GPS device has already accepted that their location is shared with Big Tech in exchange for features they value, but at least we know that any personalized info stays within Garmin instead of proliferating even further.

This is cool but requires both a Garmin product and the Waze app. IMHO better to equip new cars and trucks with bicycle and pedestrian detection.

Garmin LiveTrack itself is free for users with compatible Garmin devices and previously allowed cyclists to share their live location, speed, route, and other information with friends and family. I’ve used it myself as a safety feature when venturing off-road and on longer solo journeys. The Waze integration essentially expands that safety net to nearby motorists.

There’s obviously one big limitation: You need to be riding with a compatible Garmin device, and the driver needs to be using Waze.

But with Waze claiming around 200 million users globally and Garmin being one of the biggest names in cycling computers and fitness watches, that’s not exactly a tiny Venn diagram.

Anything that gives drivers another chance to see cyclists before actually seeing them sounds like a win to me.

#4532. Can one intense workout per week keep you healthy? Here’s the science.

Published Nov 12, 2026 8:53 AM EST

The so-called “weekend warrior” exercise approach offers an enticing trade: skip the workouts all week, and cram them into one or two days instead. It sounded great to me, until I realized it could turn my hard-earned “Thank God it’s Friday” into “Oh God, it’s Friday.”

Still, for people who genuinely lack the time to exercise during the workweek, this approach could offer real convenience—and real health benefits.

A recent study in Hong Kong has supported that idea, finding that people who packed all their weekly exercise into one high-intensity interval training (HIIT) session lost about as much body fat as those who spread the same workout across three sessions.

So, is doing all your exercise in one session really just as good as spreading it out? The answer depends on your goals and overall health. But according to Dr. Keith Diaz, an exercise physiologist at Columbia University, even infrequent exercise has real value.

“You don’t have to be a daily gym goer to reap the benefits,” he says. “Some exercise, even if it’s just one time a week, provides health benefits.”

The study, published in Nature Communications, spent 16 weeks following 315 adults who were overweight or had central obesity. The researchers split the participants into three groups, with one doing a single 75-minute HIIT session per week, and another spreading this exercise across three weekly sessions.

“They had participants do three 25-minute HIIT sessions of 4 minutes hard and 3 minutes easy,” Diaz says. “There was 15 to 30 minutes between HIIT sessions, plus a 5-minute warm-up and 5-minute cool-down.” The once-weekly group did all three of those 25-minute blocks in a single visit; the second group spread them into three visits across the week, one block per visit. A third group, the controls, did not exercise, and instead attended health education classes.

By the end of the 16 weeks, both HIIT groups had lost more body fat than the control group. Specifically, the once-weekly group lost about 1.75 pounds more than the control group, and the group that exercised three times a week lost 2.2 pounds more. Waist circumference, which is a measure of central obesity, also improved significantly in both exercise groups compared to control.

“These were relatively modest reductions in fat,” Diaz says. Neither group reported any exercise-related injuries.

The researchers measured much more than fat loss. They also tracked cardiorespiratory fitness, which is a measure of how efficiently the body uses oxygen during exercise, and a strong predictor of long-term health.

By this measure, the two workout groups did not perform equally. The group that exercised three times a week achieved roughly an 11 percent improvement in cardiorespiratory fitness, compared with an approximate 6 percent improvement in the once-weekly group. Diaz has a theory for why this might be the case.

“Physiologically, the more frequently you stress your body with exercise, the more it will adapt and yield changes to your heart, blood vessels, and muscles,” he says.

So, if fat loss is your main priority, a “weekend warrior” workout might be enough. However, Diaz believes the study actually makes a case for spreading exercise across the week “if your focus is on being fitter and generally being more healthy.”

So who does stand to benefit from squeezing a week’s worth of exercise into one session? According to Diaz, the ideal “weekend warrior” is a healthy person who, because of the demands of their daily lives, might not get around to exercising otherwise.

“This approach is best suited for generally healthy individuals who are short on time during the week and struggle to exercise because of their busy weekday schedule,” he says.

However, some people with preexisting health conditions might not see the most benefit from this highly consolidated regimen. In particular, Diaz says people with diabetes or hypertension should try to be physically active every day.

“Exercise lowers blood sugar and blood pressure for 12 to 24 hours afterward,” he says. “So, the weekend warrior approach would not be ideally suitable for individuals with diabetes or hypertension, who need these regular reductions in blood sugar or blood pressure.” Diaz adds that people with heart conditions should discuss once-weekly HIIT with their doctors before starting.

Do rage workouts really help to blow off steam?

Should you work out on an empty stomach? Fitness experts weigh in.

How much exercise do I need to stay healthy?

Although the once-weekly approach has undeniable appeal and might truly benefit some busy folks, Diaz notes that it’s not exactly the magical quick fix some headlines would suggest.

“I think the headlines around one day of exercise a week melting belly fat are misleading,” he says. “Yes, it’s one day of exercise, but it’s a lot in one day.”

Although the exercise itself takes 75 minutes in total, adding time to warm up and rest between the sessions means that the single weekly workout takes almost three hours to complete. And it’s not melting the fat away.

Despite that deflating reality check, Diaz sees real potential in this approach when healthy people use it appropriately.

“This study adds further support that some exercise, even if just on the weekend, is better than none,” he says. “So if the weekend is the only time you have to exercise, this could be an option for you.”

BMW put the i3 to the ultimate test of efficiency, charging speed, and long-distance EV capability on a nearly 3,700-mile Pan-European journey.

The Paneurpeana, as it’s called, is considered the benchmark for range and charging speed. The route begins at the North Cape in Norway, the northernmost point of continental Europe you can reach by car, and ends in Tarifa, Spain, the southernmost point of mainland Europe.

BMW drove the new i3 50 xDrive for a total of 3,658 miles (5,886.7 km) across eight countries and spent just 2 hours, 45 minutes, and 54 seconds charging at an average of 275 kW.

BMW said the charging points were not predetermined and that it had to account for external factors such as weather and traffic jams.

BMW said the trip took 3 days, 2 hours, and 41 minutes, with an average speed of 79.7 km/h, and that the i3 was charged exclusively at public charging points across national charging networks.

The vehicle was driven at all times by a single driver and was not modified in any way, in terms of hardware or software, from the standard i3 available for purchase.

The Sprinter is not your typical Mercedes. It's built for utility first and foremost, which helps explain the base model's underwhelming tech setup. Mercedes provides an AM/FM radio that plays through five speakers (13 in passenger vans).

Shoppers can option a 10.3-inch touchscreen, though, and that system supports wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto connections.

The majority of the Sprinter's driver-assistance features are optional, not standard.

For information about the Sprinter's crash-test results, visit the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) and Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) websites.

The Sprinter's limited warranty is typical for the class, but its powertrain coverage is longer than most. Mercedes doesn't include scheduled maintenance.

#4527. Tested: The 2027 BMW i7 60 xDrive Exemplifies EV Luxury

BMW’s largest executive sedan remains well suited to battery-electric power.

Taking a classic nameplate and turning it electric is a gamble for most automakers. For BMW, offering identical versions of the same model with gas-powered and all-electric powertrains has become a familiar formula. First launched in 2023, the BMW i7 has already earned plenty of love because of its smooth and silent demeanor. Can an all-new interior design philosophy cement its legacy?

Our expert editors test every vehicle we review. Read more about how we test and review cars here.

The BMW i7’s core blueprint is unchanged for 2027, but the new front end is obvious at first glance. More handsome horizontal grille slats connect a still-oversized kidney grille, while extended LED taillights connect the rear end. Inside, the BMW i7 features an updated operating system, a sleek panoramic display, and a dose of Neue Klasse styling.

Powertrain layout: 1 rear electric motor, 1 front electric motor

The mission of an extended-wheelbase executive sedan is poise, and the BMW i7 succeeds at delivering a soothing experience. Yet, powered by a 112.5-kWh battery pack, the i7 60 xDrive is also plenty fast. With 536 horsepower and 549 lb-ft of torque on tap, the i7 60 xDrive offered a surprising punch of performance.

Acceleration was swift—my experience matching BMW’s claim of a 4.6-second 0 to 60 mph—yet also dignified. Using a rear-biased, dual-electric-motor setup, the i7 doled out power in a more linear fashion than most electric vehicles. Peak torque arrived instantly and offered a genuine punch off the line, but I appreciated the more subtle wave of urge available at half-throttle and higher speeds. It felt quick enough to escape an entourage of paparazzi, but not so fast that an executive would be jostled in the rear seat by acceleration. A piped-in, synthesized sound that accompanied hard acceleration was the only sonic nod to speed.

At 6000 pounds, the BMW i7 is heavy. Even with BMW’s full suite of adaptive chassis control systems, including full air suspension and active roll stabilization, the i7 displayed its weight while winding through Orange County’s Ortega Highway. Akin to my experience in BMW’s new iX5, the electric sedan behaved appropriately but was clearly making full use of its electronic dynamic aids. Turn-in was quick enough and the steering weighted up nicely, but I could feel the active roll stabilization fighting to keep the front end pointed the right way. Similarly, midcorner bumps tended to unsettle the rear end into a quickly corrected side step. Steering feel was nowhere to be found either. But in a modern BMW, that’s no surprise, sadly.

Open highway miles were the i7’s comfort zone during my drive. The same heft that made the i7 uncertain in the canyons aided a silken ride, even on California’s disjointed highways. Like the 740, the i7 can decouple its roll bars to reduce unwanted in-cabin movement at higher speeds, and the suspension trick worked well in practice. The i7 felt soft yet secure even at a rapid cruise. Similarly, the 126.6-inch-wheelbase sedan belied its size around town, maneuvering confidently into tight parking spots and narrow urban alleys thanks to standard rear-wheel steering.

Being an EV, regenerative braking did much of the work in slowing this beastly sedan. The mechanical hardware required a stiff stab of the pedal to adequately slow down the Bimmer. However, regeneration kept the three-ton sedan in check while descending, especially when switched into the Medium or High setting.

BMW claims the i7 60 xDrive can do around 350 miles on a single charge. While I didn’t get a chance to charge it, the i7 proved to be fairly efficient during my test drive, reporting a little over three miles per kWh. Even with a mix of highway driving, canyon carving, and suburban crawling, the i7 maintained that efficiency level with little fluctuation.

The 2027 BMW i7 exhibited its biggest upgrades inside. The Panoramic iDrive system is the core of the new Neue Klasse interiors. Gone are physical iDrive controls, instead replaced by a full touchscreen system, operating on a 17.9-inch central infotainment display. An optional recessed 14.6-inch passenger screen is also available for the 2027 model year.

The glamour of BMW’s new system is tempered by a responsive but busy user experience. BMW earns points for adding a scrolling volume control near the nub shifter, but everything else is manipulated through the central touchscreen. There was a permanent menu with obvious icons for climate control, vehicle settings, navigation, and media inputs, but pressing any of these icons only started a multi-step process. Adjusting drive dynamics or climate controls required sifting through multiple menus. Despite these gripes, the responsiveness of the system was rapid, and owners will get used to the navigation over time. Shortcut functions can also be created and assigned.

BMW’s new projected dashboard illuminated necessary information across a span of masked glass on the dashboard, and the placement was nearly perfect for me. The speedometer was placed directly in front of me, while navigation and other secondary information was projected to the right. My only tactile complaint was the oddly shaped M Sport steering wheel. It is better than the four-spoke option we’ve tested on other modern BMWs, but not by much.

My two-tone i7 60 xDrive was appointed with Black Merino leather seats that were heated, cooled, and massaging. The seating experience was comfortable, though a loud fan noise from the ventilated seats was exacerbated in the otherwise-quiet EV. The plush leather seats were generously wide, and the equipped Dolby Atmos system was sonically satisfying. Interior sound levels were exceptionally low, except for the occasional speaker-based acceleration blurt.

The electric luxury sedan is a fairly full market, but the BMW i7 sits at the top of the spectrum alongside the Porsche Taycan and Lucid Air. At a base price of $108,800 (in 50 xDrive form), the i7 meets Lucid and Porsche in the middle. The Taycan starts at $114,250 with significantly more dynamic performance but less interior space. A base Lucid Air is a mere $72,400. For those looking for the benefits of BMW’s new architecture, the all-new i3 sedan offers a sharper driving experience and better range for significant savings but at the sacrifice of the first-class cabin space.

Choosing between a gas-powered and electric 7-series is arguably the harder decision. Battery-electric powertrains suit the luxury-liner mission well, and the i7 offers more power than the currently available gasoline 7-series trims. Further muddying the water is a slim $8000 delta between the base model gas 7-series and a lightly appointed i7. Ultimately, the decision will likely come down to driving range and performance desires.

Adjustable regenerative braking forces can be difficult to get just right, but BMW’s three-prong approach is nearly perfect. BMW offers Low, Medium, and High settings, all of which have distinct levels of braking force, plus an adaptive setting that uses a forward-facing camera to actively adjust retardation levels for traffic conditions.

#4526. Bald eagles Shadow and Kaydee take on a ‘nestoration’ project

Published Nov 12, 2026 11:10 AM EST

As nesting season in Big Bear Valley continues, internet-famous bald eagle (Haliaeetus leucocephalus) father Shadow and his potential new partner Kaydee are putting in the work. Like any couple, the pair is taking on a little “nestoration” project. Kaydee focused on rearranging a few errant sticks and Shadow inspected several parts of the nest.

According to Friends of Big Bear Valley (FOBBV), the nonprofit organization that runs the nest camera, this task looked physically taxing.

“For a short time, Shadow’s tongue could be seen hanging out, a behavior eagles use to help cool themselves,” FOBBV writes. “Since bald eagles do not have sweat glands, they rely on thermoregulation by ‘panting’ to regulate their body temperature.”

The birds then quietly listened to the sounds of the valley, while remaining alert for any potential intruders like the eagle they encountered earlier this week. They managed to chase off that would-be interloper.

Kaydee eventually turned around from her watch, and Shadow showered her with “affectionate little nibbles,” before moving to the front porch of the nest. Shadow stood on the back porch to watch over their territory. They then enjoyed the morning sunshine for over an hour while guarding their home.

Later in the day, Kaydee flew in from a branch called the lookout snag to the nest. When she arrived, she loudly announced her presence before flying off once again. Three other eagles were observed flying across the territory shortly after she left.

“It is encouraging to see Shadow and Kaydee working together to defend their territory while continuing to strengthen their bond,” FOBBV writes. “Watching this devoted pair grow closer with each passing day is truly a joy!”

We still do not know if Shadow and Kaydee will mate this season. Bald eagle nesting begins in September, and lasts over six months. Any eggs are generally laid in January. Viewers can follow Shadow and Kaydee and their journey on the nest via a 24/7 livestream.

Kaydee, formerly known as KD1, is a banded female bald eagle that has been spotted in Big Bear Valley following the death of Shadow’s former partner, Jackie. She was born in 2022, about 70 miles away from Big Bear Lake in the Prado Basin between Anaheim and Riverside, California. Coincidentally, her parents are also named Lucky and Ricky like Jackie’s parents, but they are a different eagle pair.

Kaydee was banded as part of the Orange County Water District’s work to track the eagles born in the area. These bands help biologists track and monitor the birds over time. Kaydee currently has a black spot on her head, but that may not be permanent. It’s possible that not all of her white feathers have come in or it could be tree sap or dirt. She also has two small bands on her legs. One is a small metal band, while the other is a lavender band with “KD1” on it.

Kaydee is almost five years old, so she is just about ready to mate.

In January, Jackie laid two eggs in the nest, but ravens destroyed them. She later laid two more eggs that hatched in April and named Luna and Sandy. The name Sandy is in honor of FOBBV’s former executive director Sandy Steers who died from cancer in February.

On July 17, Jackie was found injured on the ground near Dana Point Park, California. Cell phone video from a witness confirmed that she had an altercation with two other subadult eagles. She successfully fended off the other eagles by turning over and using her talons, but could not fly far away.

She was transferred to the Ojai Raptor Center for care, where she was diagnosed with severe anemia. Her anemia worsened during the first week of August, the Ojai Raptor Center said that she was in unstable condition on August 9. Her packed cell volume (PCV) fell below percent, before rising to nine percent. Jackie died early in the morning on August 10. The necropsy did not reveal a single cause of death, and instead pointed to several factors including severe anemia, bird flu, blood clots in her wing and one kidney, and liver and lung abnormalities.

A memorial service was held on September 5 in Fawnskin, California, along with a second celebration of life called Wings Over Big Bear on October 3. The event featured representatives from FOBBV, the Yuhaaviatam of San Manuel Nation, and more.

In November, the Ojai Raptor Center announced a “room filled with kindness,” that is covered with thousands of letters, drawings, cards, and well-wishes they have received in honor of Jackie.

#4524. BYD and Geely approached FIA about a 12th F1 team, says Ben Sulayem

BYD and Geely have both approached the FIA about entering Formula 1, the sport’s governing body confirmed. FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem named the two Chinese automakers while speaking at the New Economy Forum in Madrid, as first reported by Grande Prêmio.

But there’s no open process for a 12th team, and neither company has a deal. The FIA is also pushing F1 toward the kind of engine an EV maker has the least reason to build.

“One of them was BYD and another was Geely,” Ben Sulayem said of the manufacturers that have reached out about joining the grid.

He said he suggested that BYD buy an existing team instead of starting a new one. BYD wasn’t interested in that route. It wants its own team, so Ben Sulayem told the company to come back with a “serious proposal” that shows the project can work.

He also made it clear that Chinese manufacturers won’t get special treatment. Any bid would go through the same process as other prospective entrants, and the rules won’t be rewritten to suit them. Right now, there’s no expansion process at all: the FIA isn’t actively looking for a 12th team.

Still, Ben Sulayem repeated that he’d like F1’s next newcomer to come from China, pointing to the country’s EV technology and the Chinese Grand Prix in Shanghai.

This isn’t new for BYD. Back in March, we reported that BYD was exploring a Formula 1 entry, either by buying a team or building one from scratch.

In April, executive vice president Stella Li said BYD had met F1 CEO Stefano Domenicali in Shanghai and that an entry was “something we’re discussing.” By July, the tone had cooled. Li said “the dream is always there, but we don’t have a concrete agenda,” and special advisor Alfredo Altavilla set a clear condition: “We will never participate in Formula 1 just to put a sticker on the side of a car.”

Altavilla said BYD would only consider F1 to the extent its technology can serve the sport.

Geely is the new name here. The group sold 3.02 million vehicles last year and owns Volvo, Polestar, and Lotus, a brand with decades of F1 history. It’s also heading into Canada next year as Chinese automakers push hard into new markets.

The last newcomer, Cadillac, took a long road. The FIA opened an expression-of-interest process in 2023, and GM’s team only joined the grid as the 11th team this season, running Ferrari power until its own power unit arrives. Audi got in the other way, by taking over Sauber.

Here’s where it gets awkward for an EV maker. The 2026 F1 power units split output roughly 50/50 between the combustion engine and electric power, with the MGU-K jumping to 350 kW.

The FIA is already walking that back. In June, it agreed to shift the split to 60-40 in favor of combustion for 2027 and 2028. And Ben Sulayem has been pushing for V8 engines running on sustainable fuel with “minor electrification” for the next rules cycle, starting in 2031 at the latest, possibly 2030. Domenicali says F1 should have a package ready to discuss by the end of this year.

So the FIA president wants a Chinese EV maker on the grid, while pushing a rulebook that makes their main strength less relevant.

We like the idea of BYD or Geely in F1. Chinese automakers have the money and the engineers, and they badly need brand prestige outside China. BYD in particular has been on a performance push with Yangwang, and F1 would be the loudest possible way to tell Europe it’s not just a cheap car brand.

they look for visibility/recognition on the world stage, regardless EVs. And in some (primitive) markets they market themselves as hybrids automakers, not as EV automakers.

They will make a hybrid power unit (which they already make anyway) to comply with the backward F1 regulations.

But Ben Sulayem’s comments don’t move things much. There’s no entry process, BYD has already turned down his main suggestion, and Geely’s interest is a name dropped at a conference, not a bid.

A Chinese would likely be good for F1 as well. Motorsports are on the rise in China, and that would be the cherry on top in helping popularize the sport in the world’s largest market.

The bigger issue is the engine. Altavilla was clear that BYD isn’t interested in slapping a logo on a car. It wants F1 to showcase its technology, and BYD’s technology is batteries and electric drive. The FIA’s V8 push goes the other way. It’s hard to sell an EV giant on a sport that’s reducing the electric part of the powertrain.

If you’re following how fast EV tech is moving, from BYD’s batteries to F1’s hybrid power units, you can put some of that tech to work at home: pairing an EV with rooftop solar can cut your driving costs to nearly zero. #4523. World’s first ‘dark magic mushroom’ discovered in Florida

Published Nov 12, 2026 11:59 AM EST

A mushroom recently discovered in Florida looks unassuming, but this fungus

packs a serious and surprising punch. According to mycologists writing in the journal Current Biology, Galerina indica is the first-known “dark magic mushroom,” a species featuring hefty doses of both psychedelic and poisonous compounds.

Depending on their chemical makeup, many mushrooms will do one of two things. Fungi packed with psilocybin can send users on an extensive psychedelic trip, while varieties laden with amatoxins can be poisonous. Although mycologists have long assumed a single species could hypothetically feature both traits, no one had ever documented such an example. A recent field survey changed that, however.

“I could hardly believe it. We knew it was possible, but tried not to get too excited until we did a more rigorous analysis,” Andrew Kunik, a former University of Florida plant pathologist and study co-author, said in a statement.

Evolutionary biologists suspect certain mushrooms developed their poisonous amatoxins as a protection against foraging animals, although hallucinogenic psilocybin’s emergence and purpose in fungi remains unclear. Regardless, both compounds found their way into G. indica. University of Utah mycologist and study co-author Bryn Dentinger believes that a process called horizontal gene transfer is likely to blame—although it’s a completely novel discovery.

“Horizontal gene transfer is like if we shook hands and some of my DNA incorporated into your genome,” he said. “[But] two independent horizontal gene transfer events for these specialized metabolites in one mushroom genus are unheard of.”

For as unique as G. indica is, it is very easy to miss. The small, innocuous brown mushrooms are barely the size of a thumbnail, and resemble countless other fungi.

“These mushrooms are really hard to find,” added study co-author, University of Florida plant pathologist, and state mycologist Matthew Smith. “It’s hard to differentiate them from others, even for a trained expert.”

Although difficult, documenting the specimens is not only vital to the field of mycology. It can help save lives.

“Part of my job as Florida’s state mycologist is to identify poisonous or potentially poisonous species,” explained Smith. “So it is important to know what species we have and whether they might cause problems for people or pets.”

#4522. Watch BYD’s robotic charging arm plug itself in and charge EVs in 5 minutes [Video]

BYD’s Flash Charging tech can charge an EV in as little as five minutes. Now, BYD is taking things a step further with integrated solar power and a robotic arm that plugs itself in. See how it all works in action.

After unveiling the Yangwang Altior in the UAE on Monday, its new ultra-luxury flagship electric sedan, BYD showcased its latest breakthrough technology.

The Chinese automaker launched a new integrated charging system in the Abu Dhabi desert that brings BYD’s “Three Green Dreams” to life.

In 2006, BYD president and CEO Wang Chuanfu revealed his vision of “Three Green Dreams,” including harnessing solar power to generate renewable energy, storing that energy in batteries, and replacing gas-powered vehicles with electric ones that run on clean energy.

The new charging system is the “world’s first,” according to BYD, to integrate solar power generation, energy storage, Flash Charging, and robotic charging together in one solution.

BYD’s Flash Charging tech enables a vehicle’s battery to charge from 10% to 70% in five minutes, essentially the same time it takes to fill up at a gas station. For a full recharge, or to go from 10% to 97%, it takes just nine minutes.

The new robotic charging arm automatically locates the vehicle’s charging port, opens its cover, plugs in, and then removes it once the session is over.

By combining robotic charging with its Automated Valet Parking, BYD said the new tech goes beyond automated driving and parking to the charging process itself.

Once the vehicle is parked, the robotic charging arm automatically takes over and connects it to Flash Charging without the driver even touching the cable.

A post shared by Michael Martinez (@mmichael_martinez)

Michaël Martinez, head of marketing at BYD France, posted a video (shown above) showcasing the new charging tech in action.

The integrated solution is built around BYD’s Solar-Storage-Charging (SSC) system, fusing solar energy generation, battery storage, and its 5-minute Flash Charging tech. Together, the setup captures energy from the sun, stores it, and distributes it as needed.

If they could tie this into a smart summon type of capability, where the vehicle communicates with the charger and moves the vehicle into the proper location for charging and then moves to a parking spot once charging is complete. Rental car fleets would benefit and so would those in shopping centers. There are so many possibilities and this looks far more mature that the old snake charging Tesla demoed.

BYD has over 16 years of experience in the solar industry with a portfolio that includes solar cells, modules, and systems.

Its solar division, BYD Solar, does business in over 100 countries and regions. By using solar power, BYD said, the SCC system can operate independently off-the-grid.

The new technology is part of BYD’s wider Flash Charging rollout. By the end of 2027, the company plans to deploy 6,000 Flash Charging stations globally.
